name: Jojoba oil

lead: Jojoba oil is a golden liquid wax from a desert shrub, widely used as a facial moisturiser, carrier oil and hair treatment. People use it to soften dry skin and hair and get a smoother look.

About 97 percent of it is long-chain wax esters that resemble the skin's own sebum, and it forms a stable layer on skin that reduces water loss, according to oil-comparison studies. Controlled trials on appearance are limited.

paras: It is used as a few drops on the face or hair, as a carrier for other oils, or as an ingredient in moisturisers and conditioners. Many people with oily or combination skin choose it for its light feel. It is a daily-use product judged by how skin feels over days to weeks.
Rare contact dermatitis has been reported. It is a cosmetic oil, not intended for eating.

angle.text: Jojoba oil is a liquid wax whose esters resemble skin's own sebum, so it is used as a facial moisturiser and carrier oil. It forms a stable layer that cuts moisture loss, leaving skin and hair softer and smoother.

lead: Jojoba oil is a liquid wax pressed from the seeds of Simmondsia chinensis, a shrub native to southern Arizona, southern California and northwestern Mexico. About 97 percent of it is long-chain wax esters rather than triglycerides, which makes it unusually stable and slow to go rancid.[1][2]

People use it to help skin look softer and less dry, as a light facial moisturiser or carrier oil, and on hair and scalp to add shine and reduce dryness. It is a staple of moisturisers, shampoos and conditioners, and is often described as resembling human sebum, an idea that underlies much of its popularity with people managing oily or acne-prone skin.[1][2][3]

Published research consists mostly of reviews of plant oils for skin-barrier support, laboratory work and small formulation studies; trials that test jojoba oil alone for a cosmetic outcome are scarce.[4][5][6][7]
infobox: Liquid wax; melting point about 10 C

paras: Jojoba oil makes up roughly half of the seed's weight. Although it looks like a vegetable oil, it is chemically a wax with little triglyceride; its main fatty acid is 11-eicosenoic acid, with smaller amounts of erucic and oleic acids.[1] Unrefined oil is clear golden with a faintly nutty smell, while refined oil is colourless and nearly odourless.[1]

This structure is the reason the oil is described as resistant to oxidation and heat compared with ordinary plant oils.[1][2] Grokipedia adds that the shrub tolerates drought and heat and has been cultivated in arid regions of Australia, Israel and Argentina.[2]

The O'odham people of the Sonoran Desert used jojoba oil for sores and wounds.[1] During the Second World War the United States used it as an additive in motor and gear oils.[1] Commercial interest rose in the early 1970s, when collection from wild stands led to domestication of the plant.[1]

After the United States banned imports of sperm whale oil in 1971, jojoba oil became a substitute in cosmetics and industrial products, and it has since been used in place of whale-derived ingredients such as cetyl alcohol.[1] Because the plant grows slowly and is demanding to cultivate, the oil is typically used in small-scale cosmetic and pharmaceutical products.[1]

Jojoba oil appears in lotions, facial oils, lip balms and makeup removers, and is often marketed as natural.[1] Grokipedia describes it as non-comedogenic and hypoallergenic, attributing these properties to its sebum-like composition.[2] Reviews of plant oils for barrier repair discuss jojoba alongside olive, argan, sunflower and coconut oils.[4][5] One review of cosmetic oils describes jojoba as a moisturiser and conditioner.[3]

The oil is used in shampoos, conditioners and pre-wash scalp treatments, and traditional uses included promotion of hair growth.[7][8] A 2022 review of almond, evening primrose and jojoba oils covers their cosmetic applications in dry, ageing and juvenile skin, atopic dermatitis and scalp conditions.[9]

Because of its stability, jojoba oil is widely used to dilute essential oils and other actives. A clinical study in psoriasis used a jojoba oil-based nanocarrier to deliver the retinoid tazarotene, with the aim of reducing irritation.[10]

Microscopy and transepidermal water loss (TEWL) measurements have been used to compare how several vegetable oils and paraffin oil penetrate the stratum corneum and how well they occlude the skin.[6] Reviews note that the ratio of linoleic to oleic acid in an oil is thought to influence its barrier effects, and that processing methods such as cold pressing affect what an oil contains.[5] Jojoba's wax esters differ from the triglycerides in most oils, which is why it is often treated as a separate category.[7][8] Research reviews also report antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and antibacterial activity in laboratory settings.[7][8]

Toxicity studies summarised in a 2021 review and in Grokipedia describe low acute toxicity and minimal skin irritation, with rare cases of contact dermatitis reported.[2][8] Jojoba oil is not a conventional edible oil, and product labelling generally directs it to external use. A looksmax.org thread shows users asking about drinking it with peppermint oil for beard growth; replies from other members were sceptical, and no study of ingestion for appearance outcomes was found.[11]

No clinical trial was found that tests jojoba oil alone for acne, hair or ageing outcomes. Human studies that involve it include an observational pilot study of a clay and jojoba oil facial mask in people with lesioned skin and mild acne,[12] the tazarotene nanocarrier trial in psoriasis,[10] and a randomised trial comparing oils for perineal protection in labour.[13] Barrier and penetration work in volunteers compares several vegetable oils, including jojoba, using microscopy and TEWL.[6] A 1982 letter in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology discussed the oil in dermatology.[14]

lore.intro: On T Nation threads and looksmax.org, jojoba oil comes up as a moisturiser for acne-prone skin and as a hair or beard oil, with its sebum-like structure as the usual explanation.[15][16]
